topics.name: Types of numbers, factors, HCF & LCM
obj: Classify numbers as natural, integer, rational, irrational
Find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
topics.simple: Numbers come in families — counting numbers, whole numbers with negatives, fractions and decimals, and special numbers like π that never end. HCF is the biggest number that divides into two numbers; LCM is the smallest number both fit into.
topics.detail:
Number sets: Natural numbers (ℕ): 1, 2, 3, … Integers (ℤ): …−2, −1, 0, 1, 2… Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of integers (terminating or recurring decimals: 0.5, 0.333…). Irrational numbers cannot — π, √2, e; their decimals never terminate or repeat. A prime has exactly two factors (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23…). 1 is NOT prime. 2 is the only even prime.

Prime factorisation splits a number into primes: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Write it with a factor tree or repeated division.

HCF = product of the LOWEST powers of common prime factors. LCM = product of the HIGHEST powers of ALL prime factors present. Rule that saves time: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b.
defs: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors: itself and 1.
Highest Common Factor — the largest number that divides exactly into two or more numbers.
Lowest Common Multiple — the smallest number that is a multiple of each of the numbers.
A number that cannot be written as a fraction; its decimal form never terminates or repeats.
rules: HCF uses LOWEST powers of common primes; LCM uses HIGHEST powers of all primes
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
√ of a non-square number is irrational
formulas: Find one when you know the other two
Forgetting the rule exists and restarting from scratch
method: Split each number into prime factors (factor tree)
HCF: take each common prime to its LOWEST power, multiply
LCM: take every prime to its HIGHEST power, multiply
Check: HCF × LCM should equal the product of the numbers

examples.q: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 90.
steps: HCF: common primes 2 and 3 → lowest powers 2¹ × 3² = 18
LCM: all primes at highest powers → 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360
examples.why: The prime factorisation is the DNA of a number — every divisor is built from its primes, so the HCF must be built only from shared primes.

examples.q: Two lighthouses flash every 12 s and 18 s. They flash together at noon. When is the next simultaneous flash?
steps: Need the smallest time both intervals divide → LCM
examples.why: 'Together again' questions are always LCM; 'largest equal group' questions are always HCF.

mistakes: Saying 1 is prime
Mixing up HCF and LCM — ask: 'biggest divisor?' (HCF) or 'smallest shared multiple?' (LCM)
Missing a prime from the LCM (must include primes from BOTH numbers)
Rounding √2 or π to 3.14 and then treating it as exact
tips: In word problems, the words 'together again / repeat' signal LCM; 'largest group / greatest number of identical packs' signal HCF
Show prime factorisation even if you spot the answer mentally — method marks
summary: Primes have exactly 2 factors; 2 is the only even prime
HCF = lowest powers of common primes; LCM = highest powers of all primes

cards.a: No — a prime needs exactly two factors; 1 has only one.
Yes — the only even prime number.
Rational — it equals 3/4, a fraction of integers.
No — irrational; 7 is not a perfect square.

cards.q: HCF × LCM for a and b equals…?
cards.a: a × b (the product of the two numbers).

cards.q: Write 360 as a product of primes.
Two bells toll every 8 and 12 minutes. Together at 9:00 — next together?
Largest square tile that covers a 48 cm × 36 cm rectangle exactly?
What is the key question that distinguishes HCF from LCM problems?
cards.a: 'Biggest divisor' → HCF; 'smallest shared multiple / together again' → LCM.

cards.q: Every even number greater than 2 is…?
cards.a: Composite — divisible by 2 with more than two factors.

cards.q: Why is 0.333… rational but π irrational?
cards.a: 0.333… = 1/3 exactly (recurring = fraction); π has no exact fractional form.

cards.q: Find the HCF of 2⁴×3×5² and 2²×3²×7 without multiplying out.

questions.q: Find the HCF and LCM of 126 and 180.
ms: M1: prime factorisation of one number correct (126 = 2×3²×7)
M1: prime factorisation of the other (180 = 2²×3²×5)
questions.mistake: Taking highest powers for the HCF

ms: M1: reasoning n − 1 must be a multiple

topics.name: Fractions, decimals, percentages & ratio
obj: Convert fluently between fractions, decimals, percentages
Share a quantity in a ratio
topics.simple: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three costumes for the same number: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. Ratios split quantities into parts.
topics.detail:
Conversions: fraction → decimal: divide; decimal → percentage: ×100. Percentage → fraction: write over 100 and cancel. Recurring decimals → fraction: multiply by 10ⁿ where n = repeating length, subtract, solve (see worked example).

Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100. Reverse percentages: if a price rises 20% to $240, the ORIGINAL = 240 ÷ 1.20 = $200 — never find 20% of 240 and subtract.

Ratios: to share $420 in ratio 2:5 → total parts 7, each part $60 → $120 and $300. To simplify a ratio, divide all parts by their HCF. Map scales: 1:50 000 means 1 cm = 0.5 km.
defs: A fraction out of 100 — the number of parts per hundred.
Finding the original amount before a percentage change, given the new amount.
The multiplying factor that enlarges distances on a map or drawing to real life.
rules: To undo a % increase, divide by (1 + rate); to undo a % decrease, divide by (1 − rate)
Compare with original (before) value in % change, never the new value
Ratios have no units; simplify by dividing all parts by their HCF
formulas: Using 50 as the base instead of 40
method: Identify what is given and what is asked
For reverse %: divide the new amount by the multiplier
For ratios: add parts → find one part → multiply
Check: does the answer sit between sensible bounds?

examples.q: A phone costs $340 after 15% VAT is added. Find the price before VAT.
examples.why: Dividing by 1.15 reverses the increase exactly; subtracting 15% of 340 gives 289, which is wrong.

examples.q: Divide 84 kg in the ratio 3:4.
examples.why: The 'total parts → one part → scale up' routine works for every ratio sharing question.

mistakes: Reverse percentage: subtracting the % from the new value
Forgetting the original is the base in % change
Adding ratios directly (2:5 ≠ 2+5 parts of different things — always find total parts)
Map questions: forgetting to convert cm to km
tips: Underline the word 'original' in % questions — it tells you the base
Check ratio answers: the parts must add back to the total
summary: Ratio: total parts → one part → each share
% change uses the ORIGINAL as base

cards.q: Price before 20% rise was it $240 now — original?
Map scale 1:25 000 — how many km is 4 cm?
$500 after 10% discount — what was the marked price?
Why is the reverse-percentage base wrong when you take 20% of the new price?
cards.a: 20% was applied to the ORIGINAL; the new price is 120% of it, so you must divide by 1.2.

cards.q: Population falls 5% then rises 5%. Net change?
A shop sells at 30% profit on cost price $80. Selling price?

questions.q: A laptop is sold for $765 after a 10% discount. Find the original price.
The price of rice rose 25% to $2.50/kg. Find the original price.
Divide $1320 between three people in ratio 1:3:7.

topics.name: Standard form & bounds
obj: Convert between ordinary and standard form
topics.simple: Standard form writes big or tiny numbers as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten: 300 000 = 3 × 10⁵. Bounds are the limits a rounded measurement could really lie within.
topics.detail:
Standard form: a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. Positive n for big numbers, negative for small. On calculators, 3.2E5 means 3.2 × 10⁵.

Bounds: a value rounded to the nearest unit has lower bound = value − 0.5 and upper = value + 0.5. To 2 s.f.: ±0.05 of the last digit's place; to 1 d.p.: ±0.05; to nearest 10: ±5. When MULTIPLYING bounds: use max × max for the upper bound and min × min for lower. For DIVISION: upper = max ÷ min.
defs: A number written as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10 and n an integer.
The largest value a rounded quantity could actually be.
The smallest value a rounded quantity could actually be.
Cutting off digits without rounding — error is in one direction only.
rules: Bounds: add and subtract HALF the rounding unit
formulas: Using ≤ wrongly; upper bound is exclusive
method: Count digits moved to get a between 1 and 10 — that count is n
For bounds: identify the rounding unit, halve it, add/subtract
Combine bounds per operation (max/max, min/min etc.)
Give final bound to sensible precision

examples.q: Write (a) 456 000 000 (b) 0.000 0032 in standard form.
examples.why: Moving the decimal right multiplies, so the power grows; moving left divides, so the power shrinks.

examples.q: A rectangle measures 8.3 cm by 5.6 cm, both to 1 d.p. Find the upper bound of its area.
examples.why: The biggest possible area comes from the biggest possible length AND width together.

mistakes: a = 12 or 0.4 in standard form (must be 1–10)
Sign errors with negative powers
Bounds: forgetting the upper bound is exclusive (<, not ≤)
Division bounds inverted (max ÷ min, not max ÷ max)
tips: Standard form on paper: if the number is ≥ 10 the power is positive; if < 1 it is negative
Write the bound statement (8.25 ≤ x < 8.35) before calculating — examiners award it
summary: Bounds = value ± half the rounding unit
Multiply: upper = U×U; divide: upper = U÷L

cards.q: Upper bound for area of 6.4 × 3.7 (1 d.p.)?
Why is the upper bound written with < not ≤?
cards.a: The rounded value can get arbitrarily close to the bound but never reach it (8.25 rounds to 8.3, 8.35 rounds to 8.4).

cards.q: Lower bound of 120 km measured to 2 s.f.?
Time = distance ÷ speed. Upper bound of time uses…?
The mass 0.080 kg to 2 s.f. — bounds?
Subtracting bounds: upper bound of difference?

questions.q: Evaluate (4.5 × 10⁶) × (2 × 10⁻³), giving the answer in standard form.
The mass of a planet is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. A moon is 7.35 × 10²² kg. How many times heavier is the planet?
questions.mistake: Dividing the powers the wrong way

questions.q: A journey of 250 km (2 s.f.) took 4.2 h (2 s.f.). Find bounds of the average speed.
steps: Speed upper = max distance ÷ min time = 255 ÷ 4.15 = 61.4
Speed lower = min distance ÷ max time = 245 ÷ 4.25 = 57.6
questions.mistake: Using max ÷ max for the upper bound

topics.name: Indices, surds & approximations
topics.simple: Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication: 2⁵ = 2×2×2×2×2. Surds are exact roots like √3 that we keep in root form because their decimals never end.
topics.detail:
The laws: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ · aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ · (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ · a⁰ = 1 · a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ · a^(1/n) = n-th root · a^(m/n) = (n√a)ᵐ.

Surds: √a × √b = √ab · √a/√b = √(a/b) · k√a ± m√a = (k±m)√a (like terms only). Rationalise: multiply top and bottom by the surd on the bottom — 3/√2 = 3√2/2.

Significant figures: count from the first NON-ZERO digit. 0.004 56 to 2 s.f. = 0.004 6. Estimation: round every number to 1 s.f., then compute — 498 × 3.92 ≈ 500 × 4 = 2000.
defs: The power to which a number is raised — how many times it is multiplied by itself.
An exact root that cannot be simplified to a rational number, left in root form.
Removing the surd from the bottom of a fraction by multiplying by a clever form of 1.
Digits that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit.
rules: Fractional power m/n = n-th root, then power m
Only LIKE surds add (√2 + √2 = 2√2; √2 + √3 stays as is)
Rationalise by multiplying by the conjugate/surd over itself
formulas: Doing the power before the root wrongly
Leaving a surd in the denominator
method: For surds: simplify each root first (√12 = 2√3)

examples.q: Simplify (a) 2x³ × 5x⁴ (b) (3y²)³.
examples.why: Powers add when multiplying, multiply when raising a power to a power — and the coefficient gets the power too.

examples.q: Simplify √50 + √8 − √18.
examples.why: Simplify each surd to its '√2 form' first — only then can they combine.

examples.q: Rationalise 6/√3.
examples.why: √3 × √3 = 3 — the surd self-destructs, and multiplying by √3/√3 is multiplying by 1, so nothing changes.

mistakes: Adding powers when multiplying different bases (2³ × 3⁴ ≠ 6⁷)
Forgetting the coefficient in (3y²)³ → 27y⁶ not 3y⁶
Leaving the answer as 6/√3 when the question says 'in the form k√3'
Estimating with 3 s.f. numbers — estimation means 1 s.f.
tips: Questions saying 'without using a calculator' are surd/index questions in disguise
Always check: does my surd answer combine like terms?
summary: Laws: add, subtract, multiply powers; a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ

cards.a: Exact comparison, simpler further calculation, and it is the required simplified form in exams.

questions.q: Simplify (2x⁴)³ ÷ 4x⁵.
Simplify √72 + √32, giving your answer in the form a√2.

topics.name: Expansion & factorisation
obj: Factorise into one or two brackets
Factorise quadratics and difference of squares
topics.simple: Expansion multiplies everything out; factorisation packs a expression back into brackets. They are inverse operations — like unwrapping and wrapping a gift.
topics.detail:
Expansion: a(b + c) = ab + ac. Double brackets (FOIL): (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 5x + 3x + 15 = x² + 8x + 15. Square brackets: (x + 4)² = x² + 8x + 16 — NOT x² + 16; the middle term comes from 2 × x × 4.

Factorising: always take out the HCF first. Quadratic x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). By grouping: ax + ay + bx + by = (a + b)(x + y).
defs: Writing an expression as a product of brackets/factors.
An expression a² − b² that factorises as (a − b)(a + b).
rules: Take out the HCF before anything else
x² + bx + c: numbers multiply to c, add to b
If c is negative, the numbers have opposite signs
(a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b² — never drop the middle term
formulas: Thinking x² + 49 also factorises (it does not over reals)
method: Expansion: multiply EVERY term by EVERY term
Check the middle term is right
Factorising: HCF first, then two numbers ×→c, +→b

examples.q: Expand and simplify (2x − 3)(x + 4).
examples.why: FOIL guarantees nothing is missed; combining like terms finishes it.

examples.q: Factorise 6x² − 7x − 20.
steps: Need two numbers multiplying to 6 × (−20) = −120 and adding to −7 → −15 and +8
examples.why: Splitting the middle term using the −120 pair turns any hard quadratic into simple grouping.

mistakes: Dropping the middle term in (x + a)²
Sign errors when the bracket is subtracted: 5 − (x − 2) = 5 − x + 2
Factorising before removing the HCF
Stopping at 3x(2x − 5) + 4(2x − 5) — final answer needs one bracket pair
tips: If factorising looks impossible, check for a HCF first
Always verify by expanding back — 10 seconds, guaranteed catch
summary: FOIL for expansion; HCF then pair of numbers for factorising

cards.a: No — sum of squares does not factorise over the reals.

cards.q: Factorise by grouping: ax + ay + bx + by.
Expand (x + y)(x − y) and state its name.
cards.a: x² − y² — the difference of squares.

cards.q: The two numbers for x² + x − 12 are…?

questions.q: Expand and simplify (3x − 2)(2x + 5).

topics.name: Linear & simultaneous equations
obj: Solve linear equations with fractions and brackets
Form and solve equations from word problems
Solve simultaneous equations by elimination and substitution
topics.simple: A linear equation is a puzzle with one missing number: 2x + 3 = 11 → x = 4. Simultaneous equations have two unknowns and two equations — you find the one pair that satisfies both at once.
topics.detail:
Golden rule: do the SAME thing to both sides. With fractions, multiply through by the LCM first. With brackets, expand first. Word problems: define the unknown with 'Let x = …', build the equation, solve, ANSWER IN WORDS.

Simultaneous equations: Elimination — match coefficients (multiply one or both equations), add/subtract to kill one variable, solve, substitute back. Substitution — make one variable the subject, plug into the other. Always check the pair in BOTH equations.
defs: An equation where the unknown has power 1 — its graph is a straight line.
Two or more equations in the same unknowns, solved together for one common solution.
Replacing a variable with an expression from another equation.
rules: Elimination: equalise coefficients, then add or subtract
If signs are the same → subtract; different → add
Word problems end with a sentence answer
formulas: Moving a term without changing its sign
method: Move variable terms one side, constants the other (change signs!)
Simultaneous: match coefficients → eliminate → solve → substitute → check

examples.why: Clearing fractions first turns an ugly equation into a routine one — the LCM erases all denominators in one move.

examples.q: Solve: 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 2y = 8.
steps: y-coefficients are +2 and −2: ADD the equations
examples.why: Opposite signs on y mean ADDITION kills it. Check second equation catches sign errors.

examples.q: The sum of two numbers is 25 and their difference is 7. Find them.
steps: Let numbers be x and y: x + y = 25, x − y = 7
examples.why: Word problems ARE simultaneous equations — the skill is translating 'sum' and 'difference'.

mistakes: Sign errors when moving terms across the equals sign
Elimination: adding when you should subtract
Solving only one variable and stopping
No check — always substitute back
tips: Fractional linear equation → multiply by LCM before anything else
Make the check a habit: 5 seconds per question, saves whole marks
summary: Balance both sides; clear fractions first
Opposite signs → add; same signs → subtract
Word problems: define, form, solve, answer in words

cards.q: Why multiply by LCM with fractions?
cards.a: It clears every denominator in one step, leaving a simple integer equation.

cards.q: In elimination, when do you ADD?
cards.a: When the target coefficients have OPPOSITE signs.

cards.q: When is substitution better than elimination?
cards.a: When one equation has a lone variable (coefficient 1), e.g. y = 3x − 2.

topics.name: Quadratic equations & the discriminant
obj: Solve quadratics by factorising, formula and completing the square
Use the discriminant to count roots
topics.simple: A quadratic is an equation with x² as its highest power. It can cross the x-axis twice, touch it once, or miss it completely — the discriminant tells you which without solving.
topics.detail:
Three solving routes: 1) Factorise (fastest when it works). 2) Quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac))/2a — works every time. 3) Completing the square: x² + bx → (x + b/2)² − (b/2)², giving vertex form a(x + h)² + k and the vertex (−h, k).

Discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac: Δ > 0 → two distinct real roots (graph cuts x-axis twice). Δ = 0 → one repeated root (touches). Δ < 0 → no real roots (misses; complex pair). For ax² + bx + c = 0: sum of roots = −b/a, product = c/a.
defs: An equation of degree 2: ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
b² − 4ac — determines the number and nature of roots.
When Δ = 0, the two equal roots; graph touches the x-axis at the vertex.
rules: Formula needs a, b, c with their SIGNS
Δ > 0 two roots · Δ = 0 one · Δ < 0 none
(x + h)² + k form reveals the turning point (−h, k)
method: Write in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0
For graphs: Δ tells you crossings; vertex from completing the square

examples.q: Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0.
examples.why: Perfect-square discriminant (49) is the signal the quadratic factorises nicely.

examples.q: Find k so that x² + kx + 9 = 0 has exactly one root.
examples.why: 'Exactly one root' is the exam's code for Δ = 0 — translate the condition before touching algebra.

examples.q: Complete the square for x² + 6x − 5 and state the minimum value.
examples.why: (x + 3)² ≥ 0 always, so the smallest possible value is 0 − 14.

mistakes: Quadratic formula: b = −5 but substituting +5
Forgetting to divide EVERYTHING by a before completing the square
Δ = 0 read as 'no roots' instead of 'one repeated root'
Using the formula when a clean factorisation was available (time loss)
tips: Discriminant questions rarely ask for x — read what they actually want
Sum/product of roots is the fastest check in the exam
summary: Three tools: factorise → formula → complete the square
Vertex form (x + h)² + k, minimum k at x = −h

cards.a: One repeated real root — graph touches x-axis.
No real roots (complex pair) — graph misses x-axis.

cards.q: Why do we use ± in the formula?
cards.a: The square root has two values — the parabola can cross the axis twice.

cards.q: Find k: x² − kx + 4 = 0 has one root.
A quadratic touches the x-axis at (3, 0). Its equation form?
When should you NOT bother with the formula?
cards.a: When it factorises instantly — factorising is faster and safer.

cards.q: k for equal roots of kx² + 4x + 1 = 0?

steps: Outside the roots: k ≤ −2 or k ≥ 3

topics.name: Angle facts & polygons
obj: Use all basic angle rules fluently
Find interior and exterior angles of polygons
topics.simple: Angles around a point add to 360°, on a straight line to 180°, in a triangle to 180°. Every regular polygon hides the same trick: its exterior angles always add to 360°.
topics.detail:
The toolkit: angles on a line = 180°; around a point = 360°; vertically opposite angles equal; alternate angles equal (Z-shape, parallel lines); corresponding angles equal (F-shape); co-interior angles sum to 180° (C-shape). Triangle angles sum to 180°; exterior angle = sum of two interior opposites.

Polygons: exterior angle of regular n-gon = 360°/n; interior = 180° − exterior; sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular pentagon exterior = 72°, interior = 108°. Hexagon: 60°/120°.
defs: Angles opposite each other when two lines cross — always equal.
Equal angles on opposite sides of a transversal between parallel lines (Z-shape).
All sides and all angles equal.
Angle between one side extended and the adjacent side.
rules: Exterior angles of ANY polygon sum to 360°
formulas: Forgetting it only works for REGULAR polygons
method: Mark every angle you can find using line/point/vertically-opposite rules
Bring in parallel-line rules (Z, F, C)
Triangle sum to 180° for the kill
Polygons: find n, apply exterior/interior formulas

examples.q: Find the interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides).
examples.why: Exterior angles always total 360° for ANY polygon — one division gives the regular exterior angle.

examples.q: AB is parallel to CD. A transversal makes a 118° angle at A. Find the co-interior angle at C.
examples.why: Spotting the C-shape tells you instantly which rule pays.

mistakes: Mixing alternate with corresponding shapes
Assuming a diagram is to scale — NEVER
Using 360/n interior formula on a non-regular polygon
Rounding too early in angle chains
tips: Write the reason next to each angle ('alternate angles', 'angles on a line') — mirrors the mark scheme
Polygon question? Find n first, then choose exterior or interior route
summary: Z alternate equal · F corresponding equal · C co-interior 180°

topics.name: Circle theorems
obj: State and apply all six circle theorems
Give reasons using correct theorem names
topics.simple: Points on a circle obey beautiful angle laws: an angle standing on a diameter is always 90°, angles on the same arc are equal, and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral always add to 180°.
topics.detail:
The six theorems: 1) Angle in a semicircle = 90°. 2) Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc). 3) Angles in the same segment are equal. 4) Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. 5) Angle between tangent and radius = 90°. 6) Alternate segment theorem: angle between tangent and chord = angle in the alternate segment.

Every 'find the angle' circle question is a chain of these plus triangle facts. Always NAME the theorem as your reason.
defs: A line joining two points on the circumference.
A line touching the circle at exactly one point.
A quadrilateral with all four vertices on the circle.
Region of the circle cut off by a chord.
rules: Two angles on the same arc → equal
Tangent-chord angle → equals angle in alternate segment
formulas: Applying it to the WRONG arc
method: Mark the centre; radii to any point
Hunt for equal angles on the same arc
Close gaps with triangle (180°) and cyclic quadrilateral (180°)
Write the theorem name beside each step

examples.q: A, B, C are on a circle with centre O. Angle AOB = 96°. Find angle ACB.
steps: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc AB)
examples.why: The '2×' theorem converts the easily-marked centre angle into the circumference angle.

examples.q: TA is a tangent at A, and chord AB makes angle 58° with TA. C is on the major arc. Find angle ACB.
steps: Alternate segment theorem: angle between tangent TA and chord AB = angle in alternate segment
examples.why: The alternate segment theorem is the bridge between tangent angles and circle angles.

mistakes: Using centre-angle theorem on different arcs
Forgetting the angle between tangent and radius is 90°
Not stating reasons — the mark scheme pays for reasons

topics.name: Pythagoras, SOH CAH TOA & bearings
obj: Solve right-angled triangles with trig ratios
topics.simple: Trigonometry is the mathematics of triangles: given some sides and angles, find the rest. SOH CAH TOA is the key that unlocks every right-angled triangle.

Pythagoras: a² + b² = c² (c = hypotenuse). 3D: find a face diagonal first, then the space diagonal: d² = a² + b² + c².

SOH CAH TOA: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. To find an angle: use the inverse function (sin⁻¹). Angles of elevation/depression are measured from the horizontal.

topics.simple: A straight line is fully described by its gradient (steepness) and intercept (where it crosses the y-axis). From any two points you can rebuild the whole line.

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Midpoint = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2). Distance = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) — Pythagoras in disguise.

Line equation: y = mx + c (m = gradient, c = intercept). Given a point and gradient: use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Parallel lines share m; perpendicular lines have m₁ × m₂ = −1.

Graphical solutions: solve simultaneous equations by reading the intersection; solve quadratics where the curve crosses the x-axis.

topics.name: Transformations
obj: Describe and perform all four transformations
topics.simple: A transformation moves a shape: reflection flips it, rotation spins it, translation slides it, enlargement resizes it. The description must name the type plus the exact detail (mirror line, centre+angle, vector, scale factor+centre).
topics.detail:
Reflection: state the mirror line (e.g., x = 2, y = x, y = −x). Rotation: state centre, angle, direction (e.g., 90° clockwise about (1, 2)). Translation: state the column vector. Enlargement: state scale factor AND centre; negative scale factor flips through the centre; lengths × k, areas × k².

Finding the transformation: compare a point and its image. Same orientation + same size → translation (vector between them). Flipped → reflection (mirror line = perpendicular bisector of point–image). Size changed → enlargement (k = image length ÷ object length).

topics.name: Basic probability & tree diagrams
obj: Construct and use tree diagrams for combined events
topics.simple: Probability measures chance on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For combined events, tree diagrams keep every branch organised — multiply along branches, add between them.
topics.detail:
Core: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). All probabilities of a complete set sum to 1.

Tree diagrams: for two-stage events (e.g., two balls drawn without replacement), draw branches stage by stage. Multiply ALONG a route (AND), add SEPARATE routes (OR). Without replacement: the second stage probabilities change — adjust the denominator and remaining counts. Fractions stay exact; only convert to decimals at the end if asked.
defs: Chance of an event, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
A branching picture of multi-stage outcomes with probabilities on branches.
One outcome does not affect the other (with replacement).
rules: Without replacement: update counts on stage 2
formulas: P(A or B) = sum of routes
method: Add the wanted routes; sanity-check total = 1

examples.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Find P(both red).
examples.why: Drawing without replacement changes the second draw — 4 reds become 3 among 9 balls.

examples.q: A fair coin is flipped twice. Find P(exactly one head).
examples.why: 'Exactly one' means two separate routes — each multiplied along, then added together.

mistakes: Adding along branches instead of multiplying
Forgetting the second draw changes without replacement
Converting to decimals too early and losing exactness
Probabilities not summing to 1 — always audit the tree
tips: Write fractions un-simplified along branches; simplify the final answer
Audit: all end-probabilities must add to 1

cards.a: Multiply along branches; add separate routes.

cards.a: One event does not affect the other.

cards.a: Decimals round and compound errors; fractions are exact until the end.

questions.q: A bag holds 5 green and 3 yellow counters. One is taken at random. Find P(green) and P(not green).

topics.name: Combined & conditional probability
obj: Use Venn diagrams for two events
Solve 'at least one' problems with the complement
topics.simple: Conditional probability asks: given that something already happened, what is the new chance? Venn diagrams organise overlapping groups, and complements turn horrible 'at least one' questions into easy ones.
topics.detail:
Conditional: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Read it as 'out of the B world, how much is also A?'

Venn diagrams: for two sets, the union P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) (subtract the overlap once). Fill the INTERSECTION first when building from data.

Complement trick: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). Essential for 'at least one six in four rolls' style problems.
defs: Probability of A given B — P(A | B) = P(A∩B)/P(B).
rules: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
method: Fill intersection, then the unique parts
For 'at least one': use the complement

examples.q: In a class, 60% play cricket, 50% play football, 30% play both. Find P(cricket ∪ football) and P(cricket | football).
examples.why: Subtracting the overlap stops double-counting; conditional means 'out of football players only'.

examples.q: Find P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a fair die).
examples.why: One complement beats listing 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 routes.

mistakes: Double-counting the intersection in unions
Conditional divided by the wrong probability
Forgetting complements exist and grinding through long routes
Assuming independence when the question says without replacement
tips: 'Given that' always means conditional — shrink the sample space
Venn first, formula second — the diagram decides the formula
